title: The Economy Grows, but Americans Feel Worse About It

source.author: Jim Tyson
source.title: Economic optimism plunges to lowest level since Great Recession
source.checked_against: Single source: a news report of surveys by Gallup, Harris, the University of Michigan, the Commerce Department and NABE. Figures come only from this article; the original surveys were not opened. The link to the November 3 elections, the motor vehicle figure, the quotes from Pantheon about tax refunds and energy prices, the 3% wage figure, last month's 2.1% growth forecast, and the Group of Seven remark are left out. 'Optimistic' is written as 'positive', 'recession' as 'a serious fall in the economy', and 'economists' as 'business experts' to stay inside the reader's vocabulary.

paragraphs: The American economy is still growing. Nevertheless, Americans feel worse about it than they have for many years. That is the surprising result of a new survey by Gallup, and Retail Dive reported it last week.

Gallup asks adults every year how they see the economy. Last year, 47 percent of American adults felt positive about it. This year, only 29 percent do. That is the lowest level since Gallup started this poll in 2007. In other words, public confidence has collapsed in one year.

The last time the mood fell so sharply was during the Great Recession, from 2007 to 2009. Back then, the dark mood was accompanied by a real collapse in the financial system. This time, the mood does not correspond to the figures, because the economy is not getting smaller.

Why are people so unhappy? Gallup points to inflation. Prices have kept rising, and wages have not kept pace with them. Since 2022, Gallup says, the public perception of the economy has moved away from the real figures. That was when inflation jumped and wage growth slowed.

There is also some confusion. In a Harris poll last month, three out of four Americans said they feared a serious fall in the economy. In the same poll, 61 percent believed that such a fall had already started. That notion is wrong. Contrary to this perception, the economy has grown this year.

A survey by the University of Michigan shows a similar picture. Consumer confidence rose 6 percent this month, comparing November with October. However, it is still 10 percent below the level of February. About 57 percent of people in the survey said that high prices had hurt their standard of living.

The stores offer a reflection of this mood. Sales in American stores grew only 0.2 percent in October, after a rise of 0.8 percent in September. Spending at furniture stores fell 2.3 percent in October. In September, furniture sales had risen 3.6 percent. Olivia Cross, an expert at a research company, says that things will probably get worse. She expects consumer spending to become weaker before the end of the year.

Business experts see the economy differently. It grew faster than expected from July to September. That was partly because companies invested a lot in artificial intelligence. A group of business experts now expects the economy to grow 2.4 percent this year. More than half of them think a serious fall is unlikely before 2029.

So it helps to distinguish two things: the economy in the figures and the economy at home. The growth figures look steady, and the notion of a coming crash does not correspond to them. Nevertheless, strong growth has not been accompanied by a better mood. Most families do not distinguish between a growing economy and more money at home. Their mood is a reflection of prices and wages. As long as wages stay behind inflation, the confusion will probably continue.
